standard.title: Physical Conditions and Survival
standard.description: investigate the physical conditions of a habitat and analyse how the growth and survival of living things is affected by changing physical conditions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain how structural features and behaviours enable survival in specific habitats (AC9S5U01). They have not yet systematically investigated physical conditions as variables, examined how changes in conditions affect growth and survival, or analysed the impact of human-caused condition changes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify physical conditions in habitats (temperature, light, salinity, soil type, moisture), investigate how changes in those conditions affect the growth and survival of living things, and analyse how human-caused condition changes affect organisms — including predicting impacts and examining responses.

nodes.label: Habitats have measurable physical conditions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the physical conditions of an aquatic or terrestrial habitat — including temperature, light availability, salinity, soil type, moisture and pH — and explain how these conditions vary over time.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least three physical conditions of a named habitat and describe how at least one condition changes over time.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify the full range of physical conditions in a habitat, measure or gather data on those conditions, describe how conditions vary seasonally or in response to events, and explain why these conditions determine which organisms can survive in the habitat.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' knowledge of the physical conditions necessary for the survival of certain plants and animals — examining how deep observational knowledge of conditions guides land and resource management
Use digital sensors (soil moisture probes, digital thermometers) to collect physical condition data over time and identify patterns in condition variation
Compare physical conditions across two contrasting habitats and predict which organisms could survive in each, and which could not
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying physical conditions as named, measurable variables is prerequisite for Node 2 analysis — students who think of habitat only as 'where an animal lives' cannot analyse how a change in a specific condition (e.g. salinity, temperature) affects growth or survival. This vocabulary and conceptual shift must precede any investigation or analysis work.

response_modes.reason: First Nations knowledge of condition-organism relationships provides a sophisticated and culturally grounded direction. Digital sensor data collection over time introduces a richer data-gathering approach that connects to real ecological monitoring practice. Breadth of habitat examples reinforces the named physical conditions vocabulary across varied contexts, addressing the hinge risk.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations knowledge of condition-organism relationships provides a sophisticated and culturally grounded direction. Digital sensor data collection over time introduces a richer data-gathering approach that connects to real ecological monitoring practice.
success_criteria: Identifies at least three physical conditions of a named habitat
Explains how at least one physical condition varies over time in the habitat

nodes.label: Changing physical conditions affect growth and survival
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how changes in physical conditions affect the growth and survival of living things — using investigation data or case study evidence to support their analysis.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe how a change in one physical condition (e.g. temperature, salinity, light) affects the growth or survival of a named organism, using evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate how changes in physical conditions (salinity, soil type, sunlight, temperature) affect plant growth; examine how temperature, light and rainfall changes affect animals; explain the mechanism by which each condition change affects the organism; and use data to support their analysis.
wider: Investigate how changes in physical conditions affect the growth of bread mould colonies in sealed bags — examining temperature, moisture and light as variables in a controlled investigation
Examine how changes in physical conditions (temperature, light availability, acidity) affect corals, honey bees or flying foxes — connecting condition change to real threatened species
Recognise how environmental conditions affect life stages — ponds drying up preventing tadpole development, seeds requiring water to germinate, temperature affecting egg hatching
nodes.hinge_reason: Condition-change analysis (mechanism + evidence) is the direct prerequisite for Node 3 — students must be able to explain how a specific condition change affects an organism before they can analyse human-caused condition changes and predict organism impacts. Without this analytical move, N3 reduces to listing human impacts without explanatory depth.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly understand that extreme conditions kill organisms but miss the subtler effects of condition change on growth rates, reproductive success and life stage completion. Encountering condition-response relationships across plant and animal examples, and across different physical variables, builds a more complete analytical model.

success_criteria: Describes how a change in a named physical condition affects the growth or survival of a named organism
Uses evidence (investigation data or case study) to support the analysis

nodes.label: Human activity changes physical conditions and affects living things
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how human-caused changes to physical conditions affect living things, examine community and scientific responses, and predict the impact of specific condition changes on named organisms.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe one example of how human activity changes physical conditions and explain the effect on at least one organism.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine multiple examples of human-caused condition change (urban lighting affecting nocturnal animals, pollution changing water chemistry, habitat clearing changing temperature and moisture), explain the mechanism by which each change affects organisms, and describe scientific or community responses.
wider: Research the impacts of light pollution and how communities have used scientific knowledge to reduce it — examining covered streetlights, automated systems and motion sensors as evidence-based responses (AC9S6H02)
Investigate how changes in physical conditions caused by human activity affect aquatic organisms — examining noise pollution, temperature change, chemical runoff
Examine international scientific collaboration in Antarctica to understand how extreme physical conditions affect living thing survival — connecting to global climate condition change (AC9S6H01)

response_modes.reason: Students are often aware of dramatic habitat destruction but miss less visible human-caused condition changes (light pollution, noise pollution, temperature increase from urban heat islands). Varied examples help students see human impact as operating through physical condition change — a more analytical and generalisable framework than 'humans damage habitats'.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Light pollution and community responses (AC9S6H02) provide a rich cross-strand direction where scientific knowledge directly informs community decision-making. Antarctic collaboration (AC9S6H01) connects the concept to international science at the frontier.
success_criteria: Describes a human-caused change to a physical condition and its effect on a named organism, with the mechanism explained
Describes at least one scientific or community response to a human-caused condition change
